issues.legal_issue: A will that gives a widow and a later beneficiary successive interests in the same property should be construed to determine whether the widow received an absolute interest subject to defeasance by the later gift.
material_facts: The testator's will said that his wife would become malik of all his movable and immovable property without partnership, and that after her death his adopted son would become malik of that property on the same terms.
The will also said that the wife should live in the house and that the adopted son would receive proprietary rights like the testator.
The testator had no other near relations to provide for, and the adopted son had predeceased him.
The testator did not change the will during the period between its execution and his death.
The widow later bequeathed the disputed house to the respondent, and the appellant disputed the respondent's title.
issues.conclusion: The widow received an absolute interest in the property, subject to defeasance in favour of the adopted son if he survived her; because the gift over failed, the widow's interest was not cut down, and the respondent could take under her will.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be read as a whole, giving effect where possible to every expression; repeated words are presumed to have the same meaning unless a contrary intention appears, and all parts of the will and the circumstances of its execution must be considered (Indian Succession Act, 1925, ss. 86, 82 and 75). Where conflicting dispositions can be reconciled while giving effect to all the words, that construction is preferred; where two reasonable constructions exist, one leading to intestacy should be rejected in favour of one that avoids it. The word “malik” ordinarily describes full proprietary ownership, including alienation, unless the context or circumstances indicate otherwise (Sasiman Chowdhurain v. Shib Narain Chaudhury; Ram Gopal v. Nand Lal). Subbamma v. Ramanaidu was distinguished because the will and its circumstances differed.

predicates.will_construction_case: The dispute requires a court to construe a will disposing of property.
predicates.repeated_absolute_ownership_language_for: The will uses the same language of full ownership for an initial beneficiary and a later beneficiary of the same property.
predicates.later_gift_can_be_read_as_defeasance: The later beneficiary's gift can operate by ending the initial beneficiary's interest if the stated condition occurs, rather than by negating the initial gift from the outset.
predicates.alternative_reading_would_leave_property: An alternative construction would leave the property without a disposition in a circumstance addressed by the will.

issues.definition: When a will uses repeated full-ownership language for successive beneficiaries, the initial beneficiary receives an absolute interest subject to defeasance if the later gift can be reconciled with that interest or an alternative reading would leave property undisposed.

issues.legal_issue: An appellant should not be permitted to raise for the first time in the Supreme Court a mixed question of fact and law that was not pursued in the courts below absent exceptional grounds.
material_facts: The appellant alleged that the testator had made a later will dedicating the house to a temple and appointing the appellant as trustee.
The trial court found that the alleged later will had not been proved and that the testator was not of sound mind when it was said to have been executed.
The appellant did not pursue the issue before the District Court or in either stage of the High Court proceedings.
The appellant raised the issue in the Supreme Court, but the Court found no exceptional grounds for departing from its usual practice.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the appellant to raise the contention about the alleged later will.
issues.legal_principle: The Court ordinarily does not permit an appellant to raise for the first time an issue involving a mixture of fact and law when it was not raised in the courts below, unless exceptional grounds justify departing from that practice.

rule.if: supreme_court_appeal and issue_not_pursued_in_courts_below and issue_mixes_fact_and_law and no_exceptional_ground

predicates.supreme_court_appeal: The matter is an appeal before the Supreme Court.
predicates.issue_not_pursued_in_courts_below: The appellant did not pursue the issue in the lower courts.
predicates.issue_mixes_fact_and_law: Resolving the issue requires consideration of both factual matters and legal questions.
predicates.no_exceptional_ground: No exceptional circumstance is shown to justify departure from the ordinary practice.

issues.definition: In a Supreme Court appeal, a mixed issue of fact and law not pursued in the courts below is not considered when no exceptional ground justifies raising it late.
